470.title: Let memory be sweet
470.hook: let the memory of lost friends become pleasant, like old fruit (Letters 63)
470.howItsDone: Some people mark the memory of those they've lost by telling happy stories about them, and readers of Seneca sometimes use his phrase 'I have had them' when they remember.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lacrimae, the tears Seneca shed for Serenus beyond his own rule. Your line was grief is honest.

There's a moment, a while after someone dies, when their name comes up at dinner and, for the first time, people laugh. Somebody tells the story about the burnt turkey or the terrible car, and the laugh is real, and nobody feels guilty. The loss isn't smaller. The memory has changed flavor. The same sixty-third letter that holds Seneca's confession also holds the hope for this moment, borrowed from one of his own teachers, with an image from the kitchen and the cellar.
screen: `THE FIRST LAUGH AT DINNER.` → `THE MEMORY CHANGES FLAVOR.` → `AN IMAGE FROM THE CELLAR.`

segments.voice: Let us see to it, Seneca says, that the memory of those we've lost becomes a pleasure: not a wound we keep pressing, but something we're glad to return to. Then he quotes Attalus, the Stoic who taught him when he was young. The memory of dead friends, Attalus used to say, is like certain fruits that are pleasantly sharp, or like very old wine, where the bitterness itself delights us. At first the taste is mostly sting. With time, the sting becomes part of what makes it rich. Seneca adds a shift in grammar. Instead of I have lost them, think: I have had them. The friendship happened. It was real. Nothing that comes later can undo the years you were given. And a warning. Because nobody knows how long they'll keep anyone, let's enjoy our friends greedily while we have them. Think how often we've left them for some trip, some work, some trivial errand. The sweet memory starts now, in the time still shared. This path met a cousin of this on day four hundred twenty-three: figs in season. Attalus's version is the cellar, where time turns bitter into something you'd pour for a guest.

471.title: To school when old
471.hook: Seneca goes to lectures as an old man: learn as long as you don't know (Letters 76)
471.carry: learn as long as I live
471.howItsDone: People who take Seneca's advice keep learning at any age, coming to a new subject as a beginner without apology.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was iucunda memoria, the memory that turns like old wine. Your line was sweet memory.

Five days in a row now, a man long past his student years has gone to a philosopher's school in Naples and sat through the afternoon lecture. The lecturer is named Metronax. The student is Seneca. In the seventy-sixth letter he reports it to Lucilius, and he can already hear the teasing coming back: at your age? He answers it before Lucilius can finish the joke. And on the way to class, he passes a building far more crowded than the school.
screen: `FIVE DAYS AT METRONAX'S SCHOOL.` → `AT YOUR AGE?` → `A BUILDING MORE CROWDED THAN SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Seneca puts the teasing in Lucilius's mouth himself: at your age! He doesn't deny his age. He turns the question around: what could be sillier than refusing to learn because you haven't learned for a long time? Then his rule. Learning should last as long as your ignorance lasts: tamdiu discendum est, quamdiu nescias. And if we believe the proverb, he adds, that means as long as you live. There's never a day when you've finished not knowing something. On his way to the lecture, Seneca passes the theater of Naples, packed to the rafters. People crowd in to hear a flute player, or to decide who's the better musician. The philosopher's school has only a handful of listeners, and the crowd thinks those few have nothing better to do. Seneca finds this a little sad, and a little funny. He isn't saying an old person needs to catch up. The posture of a student is the posture of a living mind. Seneca on his fifth day of class is a quiet answer to anyone who thinks they're too old, too busy or too established to begin something new.

472.title: The mind heals
472.hook: in illness, the mind can lighten the body's burden (Letters 78)
472.howItsDone: People who draw on Seneca in illness follow their doctors' care and also tend the mind: keeping friends close, staying interested in something, and not adding complaint to pain.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Metronax, the teacher Seneca sat with in old age. Your line was learn as long as I live.
screen: `METRONAX — LEARN AS LONG AS I LIVE.`

segments.voice: Lucilius is sick: a lingering illness with a cough and a fever that keeps coming back, and he's tired of it. Seneca knows the feeling from the inside. As a young man, he was ill for years with a chest complaint that wore him down to almost nothing. So the seventy-eighth letter isn't a lecture from someone who's never been in bed for a month. It's from a fellow patient who made it through. He doesn't offer it in place of medicine. He offers what the mind can do while the body mends.
screen: `LUCILIUS IS SICK, AND TIRED OF IT.` → `SENECA WAS ILL FOR YEARS.` → `A FELLOW PATIENT WRITES.`

segments.voice: In his long illness, Seneca says, his studies and his friends were his medicine. Friends sat with him, talked with him, cheered him. Nothing helps a sick person more, he says, than the affection of friends. Illness brings three hard things: fear of death, bodily pain, and the loss of ordinary pleasures. The body carries the sickness. The mind can carry, or drop, much of the rest. Then a famous, and debatable, claim. Very sharp pain, he says, tends not to last long; pain that lasts long tends to be milder. The mind can withdraw some of its attention, and we make pain worse by adding complaints to it, telling ourselves how unbearable it is. Modern doctors would add a lot to this, and chronic pain is real in ways Seneca didn't describe. The gentler point is the lasting one. Don't add a second illness of the mind to the first of the body. Don't keep reciting your suffering to yourself. Remember brave people who bore worse. Stay interested in something. The body heals at its own pace; the mind can keep it kind company, instead of shouting at it.

segments.voice: Find one place in your body that aches or is tired today, a shoulder, your lower back, your eyes, and rest your attention there gently, the way you'd rest a hand on a friend's arm. 473.title: Stage kings and masks
473.hook: the rich are like stage kings: purple outside, poor inside (Letters 80)
473.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often try to judge others, and themselves, apart from wealth, titles and appearances, the way he says a buyer looks at a horse without its saddle.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was animus, the mind that keeps a sick body kind company. Your line was the mind helps.

Everyone who usually bothers Seneca has gone off to watch a public match, and for once nobody knocks on his door. In the quiet, he writes the eightieth letter, and his mind wanders to the theater. On stage, an actor in a purple robe strides forward and declares he rules over Argos. Another threatens to kill Menelaus with his own hand. Then the play ends, and the kings go home. Seneca knows exactly what that actor earns, and he thinks the same thing happens on the streets of Rome every day, without a stage.
screen: `EVERYONE'S GONE TO THE MATCH.` → `A KING IN PURPLE ON THE STAGE.` → `THEN THE PLAY ENDS.`

segments.voice: The man who stalks across the stage saying he rules Argos, Seneca says, is a slave, paid five measures of grain and five denarii. The one threatening Menelaus is paid by the day and sleeps on rags. The purple is costume. The crown is borrowed. The people carried in litters above the crowd are the same, he says. His word for their happiness is personata: masked. Take off the mask, and there may be little left to envy. When you buy a horse, Seneca points out, you have the saddle and blanket taken off, so you can see the animal. When you judge a person, don't count the estate, the clothes or the title. Weigh the person, not the wrapping. Persona was the Latin word for an actor's mask, and dictionaries trace our word person back to it. Seneca's point cuts both ways. Don't be fooled by someone else's mask, and don't confuse your own with your face. The job title, the follower count, the nice car: costumes. Useful sometimes. Not you.

segments.voice: Think of one person whose life looks enviable to you, and picture their costume: the clothes, the house, the title. Now imagine them at home after the play, robe off, sitting on the edge of the bed, and let them be a person, not a role. Then take off one piece of your own costume, and breathe as yourself.

474.title: A day accounted for
474.hook: Seneca gives his day: a cold plunge, a short run, dry bread, a nap (Letters 83)
474.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners write a plain account of their day in the evening, noting where the hours went without praising or scolding themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was persona, the mask that isn't the face. Your line was behind the mask.

What do you actually do all day? What time do you get up? What do you eat? It's what people ask anyone whose life they're curious about, and it's what Lucilius has asked Seneca. In the eighty-third letter, Seneca answers, hour by hour, with surprising honesty and quite a lot of humor at his own expense. What comes back is a day in the life of an aging Roman philosopher, and it's very ordinary.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?` → `HOUR BY HOUR, HONESTLY.` → `A DAY IN AN OLD PHILOSOPHER'S LIFE.`

segments.voice: We should live, Seneca says, as if in plain sight, as if God could look into our hearts at any time. So he'll watch himself and review his day, which he calls a most useful practice. Today, he says, is whole: nobody stole any of it. He's taken up a little running, with a young slave named Pharius as his partner. They're at the same turning point, he jokes, since both are losing teeth, and soon he won't be able to keep up. Seneca was once a great cold-water bather. He used to greet the first of January with a plunge into the canal. Then he moved to the Tiber. Then to a tub. And now, he confesses, it's a tub the sun has warmed, on his bravest days. Lunch is dry bread, no table needed, so simple there's no washing of hands afterward. Then a very short nap. Nothing heroic. What's striking is the honesty. He doesn't polish the day. He shows the decline, the jokes, the plain bread. Accounting for a day like that isn't about judging it. It's about seeing where it actually went.

475.title: Like the bees
475.hook: gather from many flowers and make honey that is your own (Letters 84)
475.howItsDone: Readers on their own path often keep notes from many sources, each one credited, and then try to put what they've learned together in their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dies solidus, a whole day with nothing stolen. Your line was my day, honestly.

Watch a bee on a summer afternoon. It doesn't stay on one flower: clover, lavender, a weed by the fence. What it carries home isn't a bouquet. In the hive, something happens to all of it, and what comes out is honey, which tastes like none of the flowers and all of them. A couple of weeks ago, Seneca told Lucilius to stop only quoting. In the eighty-fourth letter, he explains what to do instead with everything you read, and he borrows the bee to do it.
screen: `A BEE VISITS FLOWER AFTER FLOWER.` → `IT CARRIES HOME NO BOUQUET.` → `HONEY: NONE OF THEM AND ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: We should imitate the bees, Seneca says. They wander and pick the flowers suited to making honey, then arrange and sort what they've brought into the cells of the comb. Reading should range widely the same way, and what we gather should be sorted and blended into one flavor. Food that sits undigested in the stomach is just a weight, he says. Only when it's changed does it become strength and blood. Reading is the same: until it's digested, it sits in the memory, not in the mind. Even if your influences show, you should resemble them the way a child resembles a parent, not the way a portrait does. A portrait is a dead copy. A child is something new with a family face. Then the choir. Many voices sing together, high and low, men and women, with a flute among them, and from all of them one sound rises. That's what he wants for a mind: many sources, one voice. It's how this path has tried to work. Epictetus, Seneca, the Psalms, Zhuangzi, a scientist, a poet: always named, never mashed into one teaching. But the honey you make from them is yours.

476.title: Scipio's small bath
476.hook: Seneca visits Scipio's plain country house and its tiny dark bath (Letters 86)
476.howItsDone: Some people inspired by Seneca keep one part of their life deliberately plain, a meal, a room or a routine, and take pleasure in it rather than in upgrades.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was apes, the bees: gather widely, digest, and make one honey. Your line was one sound rises.

Scipio Africanus was the Roman general who beat Hannibal, the man Seneca calls the terror of Carthage. After all of it, he left Rome for a farm at Liternum, on the coast. Long afterward, Seneca goes there and stays in Scipio's own house. He looks over the stone walls and the towers, and then he finds the bath. It's tiny, and dark, and he's delighted. The eighty-sixth letter is a tour, and a little sermon on plumbing.
screen: `THE GENERAL WHO BEAT HANNIBAL.` → `A FARM AT LITERNUM.` → `A BATH, TINY AND DARK.`

segments.voice: The house is built of squared stone, with a wall around a wood and towers at both ends. Seneca writes lying in the very house of Scipio, and he has paid his respects at what people say is Scipio's tomb. Then the bath: small, narrow and dark, in the old style. The old Romans, Seneca says, didn't think a bath was warm unless it was dim. Here the man who terrified Carthage washed a body tired from farm work, under this cheap roof, on this plain floor. Now, Seneca says, people feel poor unless their walls shine with big precious mirrors, unless their pools are lined with marble, unless water pours from silver taps. In Scipio's bath there were slits rather than windows. Now people sneer at any bath that doesn't take in the sun all day through huge windows. Seneca isn't telling anyone to bathe in the dark. His point is that the great man of Rome needed very little, and lost nothing by it. Looking back on the week, from Attalus's old wine and school in old age to the stage kings, the honest timetable and the bees, the thread is plainness: honest memory, honest days, honest pleasure.
